createOrReplace.title: Cold Chain Logistics in India: 2026 Benchmarks
createOrReplace.html:
Cold chain logistics in India is a ₹1.32 lakh crore market in 2026, according to IBEF citing IMARC Group, yet only about 4% of perishables move through organised cold-chain networks. The result is waste on a national scale: fruit losses run as high as 15.05% for some crops, and the country runs roughly 10,000 reefer trucks against an estimated need of 62,000.

This matters now because the money is moving. The market is projected to reach ₹2.56 lakh crore by 2034, the government has raised PMKSY's outlay to ₹6,520 crore, and quick commerce is pushing chilled and frozen goods into every pin code. For a food processor, dairy, pharma distributor or 3PL, the question is no longer whether to build cold capacity. It is how to run the capacity you already have without losing product, power and margin.

TL;DR

  • India's cold chain logistics market was $12.56 billion in 2025 and is projected at $27.45 billion by 2034, an 8.62% CAGR (IMARC Group).
  • India has 8,815 cold storages with 402.18 lakh metric tonnes of capacity, but NCCD expects capacity to grow at only 2.2% a year to 2031.
  • Reefer trucks are the tightest link: about 10,000 on the road against a need of at least 62,000, per NCCD data reported by the International Institute of Refrigeration.
  • Post-harvest losses in fruits were worth ₹29,545.07 crore and in vegetables ₹27,459.08 crore, according to the NABCONS study tabled in the Lok Sabha.
  • Government support is real: 35% capital grants (50% in difficult areas), up to ₹10 crore per project, and a ₹1 lakh crore Agriculture Infrastructure Fund.

How big is the cold chain logistics market in India?

India's cold chain logistics market was worth ₹1.09 lakh crore ($12.56 billion) in 2025 and is estimated at ₹1.32 lakh crore ($14.16 billion) in 2026, according to IBEF, citing IMARC Group.

The growth curve is steady rather than explosive. IMARC data shows the market at $8.30 billion in 2020, $18.99 billion by 2030 and $27.45 billion by 2034. Storage dominates spend: refrigerated warehouses hold 57.4% of the market and refrigerated transportation 42.6%. By application, fruits and vegetables lead with 36.8%, followed by dairy and frozen desserts at 23.4%.

Geography is lopsided. IMARC estimates North India holds 33.6% of the market, West India 28.2%, South India 24.7% and East India only 13.5%. East India grows large volumes of vegetables and fish, so the low share is a capacity gap, not a demand gap.

How much cold storage capacity does India have?

India had 8,815 cold storages with a combined capacity of 402.18 lakh metric tonnes as of 30 June 2025, according to a PIB backgrounder on food storage infrastructure.

That is about 40.22 million metric tonnes, as the International Institute of Refrigeration notes in its summary of the National Centre for Cold-chain Development (NCCD) data. The forecast is the concern. NCCD projects capacity of almost 440 lakh metric tonnes by 2031, which works out to a CAGR of roughly 2.2%. Demand from quick commerce, processed food and pharma is rising much faster than that.

A tonnage number also hides how capacity is used and where it sits. The practical takeaway for operators: available space in your district, at the temperature band you need, matters more than the national total.

Why are reefer trucks the weakest link?

Reefer trucks are the weakest link because India runs about 10,000 refrigerated vehicles against an estimated need of at least 62,000, according to NCCD figures reported by the International Institute of Refrigeration.

The gap has barely closed in a decade. In 2015 India had approximately 9,000 reefer vehicles, an 85% infrastructure gap at the time. NCCD expects the fleet to reach about 33,000 by 2031, which would still leave it well short of the need. A cold room at the farm gate and a cold room at the city warehouse are of little use if the produce travels between them in an open truck.

Transport is not where most measured loss happens, though. The NABCONS study, cited in a December 2024 Lok Sabha answer, put fruit losses in transport from the farm at 0.27% to 1.41%. Most loss happens at harvest, sorting, storage and the market. The reefer shortage matters because it limits how far and how fast perishables can travel, which pushes farmers to sell locally at distressed prices.

What do post-harvest losses cost India?

Post-harvest losses cost India nearly $18.5 billion a year, according to an ASSOCHAM-ASCELA report covered by India CSR, with perishables accounting for a large share.

The government's own numbers come from the NABCONS study tabled in Parliament. A Lok Sabha answer from August 2024 reported loss ranges of 6.02% to 15.05% for fruits, 4.87% to 11.61% for vegetables and 3.89% to 5.92% for cereals. A December 2025 answer put the quantities lost at 7.36 million tonnes of fruits and 11.97 million tonnes of vegetables.

Livestock produce adds another ₹29,871.41 crore and plantation crops ₹16,412.56 crore, per the same December 2024 answer. At crop level, mango losses alone were valued at ₹10,581.92 crore, tomato at ₹5,921.15 crore and potato at ₹5,733.84 crore.

Which products lose the most?

Fresh fruit, tomatoes and fish lose the most, while milk loses the least, according to the NABCONS crop-wise averages reported in the August 2024 Lok Sabha answer.

Guava tops the list at 15.05%, followed by tomato at 11.61%, sapota at 9.53%, apple at 9.51%, marine fish at 8.76% and mango at 8.53%. Potato loses 5.96%. Milk sits at just 0.87%. That figure is a useful benchmark in itself: dairy moves through organised collection and chilling, and its losses are a fraction of those for fruit.

What government support is available for cold chain projects?

The main route is the Integrated Cold Chain and Value Addition Infrastructure scheme under PMKSY, which gives a 35% grant in general areas and 50% in difficult areas, up to ₹10 crore per project.

A PIB backgrounder reports that 395 cold chain projects have been approved under the scheme and 291 are complete and operational, adding 25.52 lakh metric tonnes a year of preservation capacity. In July 2025 the Cabinet approved an additional ₹1,920 crore, raising PMKSY's total outlay to ₹6,520 crore for the 15th Finance Commission cycle. Across all PMKSY components, a December 2025 Lok Sabha answer reported 1,619 projects sanctioned and 1,181 completed.

Financing helps too. The Agriculture Infrastructure Fund has a ₹1 lakh crore corpus, with collateral-free loans of up to ₹2 crore and a 3% interest subvention. By September 2025, ₹73,155 crore had been sanctioned for 1.27 lakh projects, including warehouses and cold stores, according to PIB.

How should operators run cold chain logistics better? A 6-step playbook

Adding capacity is slow. Running existing capacity well is faster and cheaper. From the way we build software for logistics and food businesses, these steps deliver the most for the effort:

  1. Instrument every chamber and vehicle. Put temperature and humidity sensors on rooms, reefers and, for high-value loads, on pallets. NCCD itself recommends IoT-enabled tracking. Data you cannot see is loss you cannot prevent.
  2. Alert on excursions, not averages. A room that averages 4°C can still spike for an hour during loading. Set alerts on duration above threshold and route them on WhatsApp to the shift lead, not to a dashboard nobody opens.
  3. Track utilisation by chamber and temperature band. Know which rooms are full, which are half empty and which are cooled for nothing. This is the basis for pricing, consolidation and power savings.
  4. Plan reefer routes and loads together. With the fleet this short, every empty or half-filled reefer trip is expensive. Combine route planning with load building and backhaul matching.
  5. Use shelf-life-based dispatch. Move from first-in-first-out to first-expiry-first-out, using arrival temperature history to estimate remaining shelf life per lot.
  6. Connect storage, transport and sales data. Forecast demand by SKU and location so produce goes into cold storage with a buyer in mind, not on hope.

What this means for Indian businesses

The numbers point one way. Capacity is growing at 2.2% a year while the market grows at 8.62%, so cold space and reefer time will stay scarce and priced accordingly. The businesses that win will not be the ones with the most chambers. They will be the ones that know, minute by minute, what is in each chamber, at what temperature, and where it is going next.

For most operators that does not need a large ERP project. It needs sensor data, a clean operational database and a few well-built tools for alerts, utilisation and dispatch. Frequently asked questions

What is cold chain logistics?

Cold chain logistics is the temperature-controlled storage and transport of perishable goods such as fruit, vegetables, dairy, meat, fish and medicines, from the point of production to the consumer. It covers pack-houses, cold storages, refrigerated warehouses, reefer trucks and last-mile cold delivery. A break at any link can spoil the whole load.

How many cold storages are there in India?

India had 8,815 cold storages with a combined capacity of 402.18 lakh metric tonnes as of 30 June 2025, according to PIB. NCCD projects capacity of almost 440 lakh metric tonnes by 2031, growth of about 2.2% a year, which is slower than demand from quick commerce, food processing and pharma.

How many reefer trucks does India need?

India needs at least 62,000 reefer trucks but has only about 10,000, according to NCCD figures reported by the International Institute of Refrigeration. The fleet is expected to reach around 33,000 by 2031. That shortage limits how far perishables can travel and pushes farmers to sell locally at lower prices.

How much food does India lose after harvest?

The NABCONS study tabled in Parliament found losses of 6.02% to 15.05% for fruits and 4.87% to 11.61% for vegetables, equal to 7.36 million tonnes of fruit and 11.97 million tonnes of vegetables. Fruit losses were valued at ₹29,545.07 crore. An ASSOCHAM-ASCELA report puts total post-harvest losses at nearly $18.5 billion a year.

What subsidy is available for a cold storage project in India?

Under the PMKSY cold chain scheme, integrated projects can get a 35% grant in general areas and 50% in difficult areas, up to ₹10 crore per project. Standalone cold storages can use MIDH or National Horticulture Board subsidies, and the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund offers loans of up to ₹2 crore with a 3% interest subvention.
